item.title: Mayors Are Filming Videos, Mamdani-Style, With Varying Degrees of Cringe
item.description:
Susana Mendoza, the Illinois state comptroller and a candidate for mayor of Chicago, was not going to let the crummy weather get in her way. She had videos to shoot.

Sheltered on a drizzly recent afternoon under the overhang of a building along the Chicago River, Ms. Mendoza, in a black suit, high heels and her signature updo, faced a cellphone held aloft by a staffer — then flubbed her line.

“I’m the only candidate for mayor with the financial management experience and backbone to manage this crisis,” she said confidently, pointing at the camera as she walked.

Tackle the crisis, an aide corrected. Ms. Mendoza clapped her hands, then jogged in reverse to try the shot once more.

“This is how it works,” she said cheerfully.

And this is how mayors and mayoral hopefuls are talking to constituents these days: with snappy, walk-and-talk, make-policy-personal videos that reach potential voters on TikTok or Instagram.

The videos’ growing popularity can be traced to New York City and Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a digital native who is widely seen as a master of the art. His campaign relied on viral social media posts to get his message out and help propel him to victory last year.

But not all candidates are as skilled on camera. Some videos are charming, real-life glimpses into the day of a mayor trying to solve problems. Others come across as stilted, overproduced or even awkward. Most candidates are learning as they go.

“They can be effective, but the person has to be genuinely likable or it doesn’t work,” said Aviva Bowen, a political strategist in Chicago. “They’re supposed to be raw and gritty and a peek behind the curtain.”

Last month, Mayor Brandon Johnson of Chicago publicized his re-election bid with a video of himself dancing, albeit stiffly, on a rooftop. Mayor Daniel Lurie of San Francisco took to video to warn residents that a mountain lion was spotted at the corner of 44th Avenue and Ulloa Street. Jacob Frey, the mayor of Minneapolis, recently showed off his between-the-legs dribble — and a few bricked jump shots — while telling residents about a basketball tournament returning to the city.

Good or bad, the videos are increasingly a staple in the day of an American mayor — or an aspiring one.

Campaign strategists say that the videos — which are also being adopted by governors, members of Congress and other elected officials — can be deceptively tricky to pull off. They are most compelling, the consensus goes, when they are candid, honest and shorter than 30 seconds. Success is measured in shares, views, likes and comments.

The videos can also help push an obscure candidate into the spotlight. In Seattle, Katie Wilson was running for mayor last year as a nearly unknown community organizer and socialist when she released a video of herself standing on a sidewalk holding an $8 slice of pizza and explaining how the cost was connected to the city’s housing crisis. Her campaign took off, and months later she was elected, unseating the incumbent, who had led Seattle since 2022.

Ms. Wilson’s videos worked because they leaned into her image as an awkward policy nerd who isn’t natural on camera, said Sandeep Kaushik, a Democratic political strategist in Seattle who was not involved with her campaign.

“They come across as really honest and authentic,” Mr. Kaushik said. “And they showed you who she is as a person. They weren’t formal or antiseptic or cerebral in the way most campaign communications are.”

Annie Gabillet, the deputy communications director who oversees digital work for Mayor Lurie in San Francisco, said that his videos are an outgrowth of the early days of his campaign. Mr. Lurie had never run for office before and was fighting for name recognition. So he began making candid, in-the-moment videos, sometimes dropping in on small businesses or art galleries, places around the city that he loved.

“He didn’t set out to become an influencer, so as he’s filmed more videos himself, it’s become more natural, as if he’s just talking to San Franciscans,” she said.

Mr. Lurie’s Instagram audience is largely San Francisco-based, and he relies on Instagram reels to get his messages out. Some of his highest-performing videos this year have been snapshots of life in the city: a new Jollibee opening on Market Street, a how-to on cleaning storm drains, a scene of Mr. Lurie stopping by a salsa dancing event in Union Square.

But mayors have to be careful to exude not just authenticity, but competence, as Mayor Karen Bass of Los Angeles learned the hard way.

After Mr. Mamdani touted his administration’s pothole-filling prowess, a Los Angeles resident posted a video asking Ms. Bass to fill a hole on her street. Ms. Bass responded with her own video — explaining why the pothole could not be addressed right away.

Social media mockery ensued. Ms. Bass followed up the next day with a video showing the fixed pothole.

“Sometimes content lands differently than you intended,” said Leslie Gamboni, senior director of digital communications for Ms. Bass, adding that the reaction didn’t necessarily make the video a failure. “We did see that the video reached a lot of people, and hopefully people came away understanding more about 311 and how to report an issue.”

As next year’s mayoral election in Chicago begins to heat up, mayoral hopefuls are elbowing each other for attention in real life — and on Instagram reels.

Alexi Giannoulias, the Illinois secretary of state and a mayoral candidate, has been making the rounds of block parties, concerts and food festivals and posting videos of his interactions with voters online.

Last month, Mr. Giannoulias shared videos of himself jumping into the Chicago River, speaking at an event celebrating Chinese heritage and downing tequila at the city’s Mexican Independence Day parade.

“Alexi believes it’s important to communicate directly to voters where they are, whether that’s knocking doors or short-form video on social media,” said Jordan Abudayyeh, a campaign spokeswoman.

Mayor Johnson, who is running for re-election, has hired social media influencers to make posts promoting his campaign, circumventing traditional media. “We hope to showcase the mayor in his element,” said Christian Perry, a campaign spokesman.

Ms. Mendoza is not on the air with television ads yet, but she drops new social videos regularly, sometimes filming several at once.

In September, as rain continued to threaten her shoot, Ms. Mendoza said that she sees the videos — which she said she had been posting long before Mr. Mamdani’s rise — as crucial to her nascent mayoral campaign, less than five months from the February election.

“When I bump into people in real life, more and more and more, they’re like, ‘Oh my gosh, I love your videos,’” she said. “They feel like they already know me. Then I get to seal the deal with them.”

Cynthia Silva contributed video research and editing.

item.title: They Argued About Trump at a Dog Park. Then They Pulled Their Guns.
item.description:
Before any criminal charges were filed, before any weapons were drawn, before anybody mentioned the president, a dog named Bob wanted to go to the park.

Bob’s owner, David Mattai, had the week off from his job as a forklift mechanic. Mr. Mattai, 55, first tried taking Bob on a hiking trail, but the spaniel refused to walk. So Mr. Mattai drove to his favorite dog park in Bainbridge, Ohio.

At a picnic table inside the park that April afternoon was Emmanuel Mathews, 80, and his corgi, Frankie.

Mr. Mathews was retired from a career as a meat distributor, and on the days when his back wasn’t causing him problems he was a regular at the park. He had brought a copy of The Wall Street Journal with headlines that included “Trump Grapples With Fears on War.”

The events that unfolded over the next 20 minutes — pieced together from interviews, records and body camera footage — would be unusual, but hardly unthinkable in a country where political tensions so often combust. Two men, one Black and liberal, one white and conservative, would disagree about President Trump. Their disagreement would become an argument, then a screaming match and then, because both men had guns in their cars, a crime.

What happened at the dog park — and who is to blame — will soon be scrutinized by a judge and a jury, as both men face the possibility of time behind bars and grapple with the lifelong consequences of division turning violent.

Likely to take the stand in both cases is Jamie Jedlinsky, 70, the singular witness to what went down.

Mr. Jedlinsky’s mother had taught him that you didn’t have to tell people who you voted for, so he never did. If someone brought up politics, he would usually change the subject to birding. But on this day, Mr. Jedlinsky and his pit mix, Willow, had walked into the park and greeted Mr. Mathews, with whom he had become somewhat friendly over the years. When he noticed the newspaper in Mr. Mathews’s hands, he decided to gesture to the headline about the Iran war and say, “That sucks, don’t it.”

Mr. Mathews, who goes by Mike, disagreed. In his cardigan, he began to discuss his support for the president’s choices.

Mr. Mattai, who had arrived moments earlier in sweatpants, was listening. He considered himself a democratic socialist before it was trendy. He owned a collection of bumper stickers with messages such as “Trump Is a Felon” and “Hicks Don’t Mix With Politics.” In his solidly Republican patch of Northeast Ohio, he considered it his moral duty to “comfort the afflicted and afflict the comfortable.”

Mr. Mattai, who had struggled with alcoholism for most of his life, would later say he had been drinking that day.

He decided to butt in. “Trump is the worst president in history,” he said, to which Mr. Mathews replied, “Trump is the best president in history.”

The spat quickly grew in intensity and volume. At one point, Mr. Jedlinsky recalled, they were saying, “You shut up!” and “No, you shut up!”

“Just two guys, mad at themselves, mad at the world,” Mr. Jedlinsky said. “They both wanted to just yell at someone, and they ran into the perfect storm, where there’s somebody yelling back.”

Mr. Jedlinsky was relieved when the younger man finally heeded his advice to both of them to let it go. Mr. Mattai leashed Bob, returned to his Hyundai and began to drive toward the park’s exit. But then Bob started to whine.

“Man, you did want to stay at the park,” Mr. Mattai recalled telling his dog. He turned his car around.

Some of the specifics of what happened next remain in dispute. But Mr. Jedlinsky, Mr. Mattai and a lawyer for Mr. Mathews agree upon a certain set of facts. (Mr. Mathews declined to be interviewed.)

Mr. Mattai entered the park again and told Mr. Mathews that he should be the one to leave. Mr. Mathews began to move toward his Cadillac, which was adorned with a corgi sticker. When he made it to the other side of the fence, he turned around.

“Did your mother drop you on your head?” he asked.

“You talking about my mother?” Mr. Mattai responded. He reached across the fence and grabbed Mr. Mathews by his grayish white hair. Mr. Jedlinsky pushed them apart and told them both to go home. While the three men were putting their dogs in their cars, Mr. Jedlinsky heard Mr. Mattai say: “Oh you’ve got one? I’ve got one, too.”

Then Mr. Jedlinsky heard gunshots.

Mr. Mathews had a .45-caliber handgun in his car. He fired first; when he pulled the trigger a second time, no bullet came out. Mr. Mattai had a 9-millimeter pistol in his car. He fired back at least four rounds. The bullets sprayed across Mr. Mathews’s car and into his open window as Mr. Mathews drove away. They pierced his door frame and the driver’s seat, missing him by inches.

Mr. Jedlinsky crouched behind his wheel and called 911.

“It escalated,” he told the dispatcher.

When a police officer arrived, he found Mr. Mattai splayed on the pavement. There was a hole in his lower back where Mr. Mathews’s bullet had entered, and another in his abdomen where it had exited.

The passenger-side door of his Hyundai was open. Bob was in the front seat, unharmed, tongue out.

Mr. Mathews peeled out of the parking lot and drove toward the Bainbridge police station. In this area of Northeast Ohio, where the Cleveland suburbs begin to meet rural farmland, Mr. Mathews was familiar with law enforcement. Before he retired, his meat company had provided burgers and cutlets for police events.

He had made it about four minutes up the road when he saw a Bainbridge police cruiser, siren on, coming toward him. Mr. Mathews stopped his car and flashed his lights. The officer pulled over.

“You going to the shooting?” Mr. Mathews asked. “I was part of it.”

The officer, whose body camera was rolling throughout their interaction, confiscated Mr. Mathews’s handgun, patted him down and removed a piece of paper from the pocket of his cardigan.

“That was my list for the day,” Mr. Mathews told the officer. “This wasn’t on it.”

He quickly informed the officer of his local connections: the cops he knew, the poker game he used to play with the former police chief, and the fact that he happened to be living with the mother of the county’s top prosecutor. Before long, Mr. Mathews was telling his side of the story from the back of the police cruiser.

He lifted his handcuffed wrists to wipe tears from his eyes. There was a small cut on his cheek. He said the other man had not just grabbed his hair, but also head-butted him before they went to their cars.

He did not say who pulled a gun out first.

“I said, ‘I feel my life is in danger.’ I said that ’cause I know that’s what they say,” Mr. Mathews told the officer. “And he went around the side of his car and started coming at me, and I shot him.”

At the police station, he kept talking as the officer confiscated the cross around his neck, the Greek coin ring on his finger and the $890 in his wallet.

“That’s a bad thing I did, but it really wasn’t,” Mr. Mathews told the officer. “This guy had a gun in his hand.”

In the back of the police car and while being booked, he asked four times about the well-being of his dog, Frankie. He did not ask about the condition of the man he had shot.

At the hospital, Mr. Mattai’s wife, Sally, couldn’t stop crying. The doctors had explained that her husband was in emergency surgery, and they couldn’t say for sure if he would make it through.

When he did, Mr. Mattai learned that the bullet had torn through his intestines and fractured his spine. He had a second surgery the next day.

It didn’t surprise his wife to learn how the confrontation at the dog park had started. It was politics, in part, that had brought her and Mr. Mattai together about a decade earlier, in a Facebook group where they shared memes.

Mr. Mattai had told her how he had immigrated from Guyana at 10, become an American citizen and joined the Marines. He worked as a paramedic in California until his alcohol addiction cost him his job. When the two met, Mr. Mattai had moved in with his father in New York and was trying to start over. He went to welding school.

When he moved to Ohio to be with Sally, they lived on nearly four acres in a rural area. They flew a Kamala Harris flag in 2024, but took it down the morning after the election. One of their neighbors, they said, kept up a cardboard cutout of Mr. Trump showing two middle fingers.

Now, Mr. Mattai's wife felt certain that what happened to him was a result of Mr. Trump’s disparaging of minorities.

“We’ve seen this movie before, the whole, ‘I feared for my life because it was a Black guy’ crap,” she said.

Her husband agreed. He initially told the police, from his hospital bed, that he had not touched Mr. Mathews and did not speak to him after seeing his gun. Mr. Mattai later told The New York Times that he had grabbed Mr. Mathews by the hair, but said that had been the extent of the physical contact.

“I was in the infantry for 10 years,” Mr. Mattai said. “If I had head-butted him, he would not have driven off anywhere.”

Though Mr. Mattai told The Times that he had served in the Marines for a decade, the Marines said his length of service was less than a year. Asked about the discrepancy, Mr. Mattai apologized, saying he had become accustomed to embellishing his military record because he was embarrassed about his past.

“It’s like the facade I made up for the world,” he said. “I didn’t want to tell them that I just, kind of, had this life of a bum.”

Two weeks after the shooting, Mr. Mattai was released from the hospital. He struggled to walk with a walker and had severe pain down the right side of his body. He needed months of rehab. But first, he had plans.

As soon as he got home, he said, he poured all his vodka down the drain. Then he went to his garage, where he kept his collection of political bumper stickers. He threw them in the trash. From then on, he said, he wasn’t going to drink and he wasn’t going to confront anyone about their political views.

Mr. Mattai concluded that it must have been God who sent Mr. Mathews and his gun to the dog park to teach him a lesson.

“I needed violence done to me to correct the path that I had put myself on,” he said.

But he still wanted to see Mr. Mathews sent to prison.

Mr. Mathews was charged with felonious assault, a second-degree felony. If convicted, he could face up to eight years in prison and would be required to serve at least three. After posting a $50,000 bond, he was released with a GPS ankle monitor.

His trial is scheduled for February. His lawyer, Ian Friedman, plans to argue that the shooting was justified. Under the “stand your ground law” passed by Ohio Republicans in 2020, someone facing an imminent threat of serious harm does not have to try to escape before using deadly force.

“This case was never about politics or any other motivation, other than Mike being faced with a life or death situation and acting to save his life,” Mr. Friedman said.

In recent years, Mr. Mathews had endured a heart attack, a stroke and two back surgeries. Now at 80, he was reckoning with the possibility of spending what could be his final years in prison.

On the day he was arrested, Mr. Mathews told the police, “I should have been more of a coward, and this wouldn’t have gone this far.”

The local prosecutor — the one whose mother lives with Mr. Mathews — recused himself from the case and brought in the Ohio Attorney General’s Office.

That office was not asked to consider potential charges against Mr. Mattai, according to a spokesman.

But in August, four months after the shooting, Mr. Mattai received a call from his lawyer telling him that there was a warrant out for his arrest. He turned himself in.

The next morning, he learned that a prosecutor from another county had been brought in on the case. The prosecutor was charging Mr. Mattai with misdemeanor assault and disorderly conduct based on Mr. Mathews’s claim that Mr. Mattai had head-butted him. Mr. Mattai faces up to six months in jail.

He said he was willing to plead guilty or no contest when he returned to court in late October, if it meant avoiding jail time. He now walks with a limp and says he can’t return to his forklift mechanic job because he is unable to lift heavy objects.

“I got my own life sentence from this,” Mr. Mattai said. He has not taken Bob back to the dog park.

Mr. Jedlinsky, the man who tried to break up the fight, spent months away from the park, too. He said he was so shaken up in the aftermath that he didn’t sleep.

He didn’t remember seeing a head butt. He couldn’t say what Mr. Mattai was doing when the bullet entered his back. He wasn’t taking sides, in this fight or any other.

“This country is in a big divide right now,” Mr. Jedlinsky lamented. “It’s, ‘You’re either with us or against us.’ You’ve got a pick a side and hate the other side.”

Mr. Jedlinsky had spent months thinking about that day when his life had been put in danger. After everything it had cost the men involved, he was certain of one thing: Nobody’s mind had been changed.

item.title: Democrats Project a Party Milestone in Congress: 100 Women in the House
item.description:
Democrats pressing to win control of Congress in the midterm elections are also reaching for a major milestone in their ranks: electing at least 100 women to the House, the most ever in a legislative body that is still heavily dominated by older white men.

With female candidates competing in many key districts that will determine the House majority, and polls showing the party gaining ground in those contests, Democrats are projecting they could have as many as 113 women in their ranks next year.

“I’m incredibly confident that we will pass that 100 mark,” Representative Teresa Leger Fernández of New Mexico, chairwoman of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said in an interview. “The real issue is how far above it do we go.”

Low-end estimate includes races rated by the Cook Political Report as favoring Democrats; high-end includes all tossups.

Ashley Wu and Elena Shao/The New York Times

The peak projection of 113 could only be reached if Democrats won every competitive race, including a few that more strongly favor Republicans, a highly unlikely scenario even in the best of years. But even reaching 100 would be a high-water mark that was unthinkable just a generation ago. When Emily’s List, the largest funder of female Democratic candidates who support abortion rights, was founded in 1985, less than 5 percent of the House Democratic Caucus were women. Now, it is approaching 50 percent.

“We have all along in this election cycle put women front and center to deliver the House majority,” said Jessica Mackler, the president of Emily’s List, who noted that women backed by the organization make up a majority of tossup House races.

That didn’t happen by accident. This year, 18 out of the 40 Democrats in the party’s “Red to Blue” program that funds top contenders in battleground districts are women.

“Women are going to give Democrats the majority in two ways,” Ms. Leger Fernández said. “We’re going to elect women candidates who will flip the House, and it’s also women voters who will come out and overwhelmingly vote for Democratic candidates, because the two hardest-hit groups by the Republicans’ policies have been Latinos and women.”

Currently, there are 97 women in the House Democratic Caucus (including two nonvoting delegates who represent Washington, D.C., and the Virgin Islands), a record for female representation accounting for around 45 percent of Democratic members.

While some are retiring, Democrats expect those who remain to be joined by a large crop of women running in safe Democratic districts and others who are strongly favored to win competitive races in an environment that polls show is favorable to their party, resulting in even higher numbers next year.

The first tier of candidates Democratic leaders are counting on includes a dozen women who are running in open or safely Democratic seats, including Melat Kiros in Colorado; Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York and Stefany Shaheen in New Hampshire.

Three others pressing to flip Republican districts are seen as very likely to win: Marni von Wilpert, who is running in a newly drawn California district; Denise Powell, who is seeking a Democratic-trending Nebraska seat currently occupied by Republican Representative Don Bacon; and Rebecca Bennett, who is polling ahead of Representative Tom Kean Jr., the lawmaker who was absent from Congress for over 100 days for what he later revealed was a struggle with depression.

A dozen more women are running in races that the nonpartisan Cook Political Report ranks as “tossups.” Ms. Leger said she was confident that three or more of them would win in November. They include challengers to some of the most vulnerable Republican incumbents, including Representatives Rob Bresnahan Jr. of Pennsylvania, Jen Kiggans of Virginia, Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin, Juan Ciscomani of Arizona, Mike Lawler of New York and Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa.

If a handful of Democratic women running to flip more Republican-leaning districts in Colorado, Florida, Iowa and South Carolina prevail, the ranks could swell even more.

Should Democrats win the majority, Ms. Leger said she expected women to be the driving force next year on an agenda focused on child care and elder care.

In her state of New Mexico, she said, “we have a majority-women legislature with a woman governor and we have universal child care; I want to see that kind of progress.”

Kelly Dittmar, a professor of political science at Rutgers University, said that representation mattered also “for perceptions of legitimacy.” A growing number of women serving in legislatures not only changes policy but “changes the institutions themselves,” she said.

As an example, Ms. Dittmar pointed to the reaction in 2020 to an episode in which Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democrat of New York, was called a “fucking bitch” by a male Republican colleague. Instead of letting it go, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez delivered a floor speech in which she read the vulgarity into the congressional record, and other female lawmakers rose to recount their own stories of experiencing sexism in the halls of power.

Ms. Leger said having more women in Congress would also be more effective than any policy change in addressing the culture of sexual harassment on Capitol Hill.

“When you have close to 50 percent of the Democratic caucus understanding what is it like to be on the other end of sexual assault, sexual mistreatment, sexual harassment, the conversation changes,” she said.

Republicans have far less gender diversity in their ranks in the House, where there are currently 32 G.O.P. women (including two nonvoting delegates) — around 15 percent of their members — and are at risk of those levels dropping further. To maintain the party’s number of female House members, it’s likely that six vulnerable G.O.P. women would have to succeed in fending off their challengers next month.

The G.O.P. is also losing much of its racial diversity in the House: All four Black Republicans serving there are leaving Congress next year.

Representative Emilia Sykes, Democrat of Ohio, said there were still small daily reminders that she served in an institution that was not designed with her in mind, even as the number of women climbed.

“The size of the chairs is a problem,” Ms. Sykes said. “I’m not a big person; sitting in the chairs that are very large, my feet dangle.”

She said she sometimes receives letters addressed to “the congressman,” which boggles her mind.

“I think, ‘OK, you’re coming to advocate for millions of dollars and significant policy changes, and you have the lack of research to know the member isn’t a man,’” she said.

Ms. Sykes said her journey to Congress as a young Black woman has been challenging: Fund-raising has been more difficult for her, she said. Consultants were quick to overlook her when she first wanted to run. But she said she was a firm believer in the mantra “if you see it, you can be it.”

“For the women who have found their way,” she added, “the fights that they’re fighting are incredible.”

item.title: Supreme Court to Hear Major Environmental Lawsuit
item.description:
Who should cover the costs of climate change?

That is the question underpinning the first case of the Supreme Court’s new term, a landmark dispute over whether state and local governments can seek to hold oil companies responsible for billions of dollars in costs from floods, droughts, wildfires and other climate-related disasters.

The case before the justices pits officials from Boulder, Colo., against two major oil companies — Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil. The Colorado officials contend that they should be able to proceed with a lawsuit arguing that the oil companies violated state law and seeking to hold them responsible for the costs of environmental damages. The companies, joined by the Trump administration, argue that such lawsuits are barred by federal law and the Constitution.

A decision is expected by the end of June or early July. Depending on its scope, the ruling could have significant implications for similar efforts to sue fossil fuel companies for billions of dollars in damages caused by climate change.

If the court sides with the companies and finds that such lawsuits are not allowed, it could doom dozens of other such cases by local and tribal governments percolating in lower courts throughout the country.

A decision for Boulder could clear the way for similar cases to move forward, potentially opening up oil companies to enormous financial liability.

Only eight of the nine justices are scheduled to take the bench for the argument. Last week, Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. announced he would recuse himself from the case.

He gave no reason in the recusal announcement, but he had faced pressure from environmental and court watchdog groups to step aside because he has publicly reported owning stock in two oil companies that are not parties to the case but could be affected by the outcome, ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. He had also gone on a luxury fishing trip with an investor in a company involved in the dispute.

In an interview after his announcement, Justice Alito told Bloomberg that he had taken “into account the particular arguments that were made on both sides here” and decided that recusal was “the prudent step.”

Under the court’s ethics code, justices can recuse at their own discretion. They typically step aside if their impartiality could be questioned, including because of a financial tie to a party or a close friend or family member who is involved.

If the justices were to split 4 to 4 in Justice Alito’s absence, a lower court decision to allow the Boulder suit to move ahead would stand. Such deadlocked decisions set no binding national precedent.

The legal fight began in April 2018, when the city and county of Boulder sued Exxon and Suncor, asserting that the companies should be required to share in the costs of climate change, including damages from more heat waves, wildfires, droughts and floods.

Boulder argued that local governments and taxpayers “cannot pay the full costs of all that is needed, nor should they.” The suit contended that the companies “knowingly and substantially” fueled the climate crisis by “producing, promoting and selling a substantial portion of the fossil fuels that are causing and exacerbating climate change.” It also claimed that the companies concealed and misrepresented the dangers of their products.

After a decision by the Colorado Supreme Court to allow the case to continue in state court, the oil companies asked the justices to intervene. The Trump administration joined them, a reversal of the Biden administration’s stance on the climate lawsuits.

The oil companies argued that the case should be heard in federal court, not state. Federal courts are often thought to be a more business-friendly venue.

The companies claim that federal laws regulating the environment pre-empt Boulder’s lawsuit and that because climate change is a global problem, it cannot be handled in state courts.

They are joined by the lawyers for the Trump administration, who argue that a ruling for Boulder could spur a raft of litigation, allowing “every locality in the country” to “sue essentially anyone in the world for contributing to global climate change.”

Boulder has pushed back on those arguments, saying in its briefs that its lawsuit is part of a tradition “since the Founding” to use state law to handle cases where the harm comes from outside the state, including in environmental cases.

item.title: Who’s winning the race for Congress?
item.description:
Supported by

It’s Oct. 5 — 29 days away from the midterms. Here’s the state of play.

By Lisa Lerer and Shane Goldmacher

“It’s a five-alarm fire.” A “slow moving car crash.” Republicans are “hemorrhaging” and “should brace for losing everything.”

Republicans have been full of doom in recent days, as they confront the reality that their political prospects do not seem to be improving. And their candidates are rapidly running out of time for a turnaround.

With less than 30 days before the election, Democrats are reaching deeper into traditionally conservative areas while Republicans find themselves fighting to save their incumbents.

Decisions last week by Republicans to pull money out of the North Carolina Senate race and divert resources to Kansas demonstrated the depth of their party’s challenge, as new New York Times/Siena University polls found strength for Democrats in five reliably Republican states that could determine control of the chamber.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Based on New York Times/Siena polls of 504 voters in Alaska conducted Sept. 24 to Oct. 1, 606 voters in Iowa conducted Sept. 22 to Oct. 1, 605 voters in Kansas conducted Sept. 22 to 30, 616 voters in Ohio conducted Sept. 22 to Oct. 1 and 615 voters in Texas conducted Sept. 21 to 30.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

The first events in what President Trump has promised will be a series of midterm appearances — all in deep red states — underscored the anxiety among Republicans that even some of their most loyal voters could stay home from the polls in November.

And a series of economic indicators released last week, showing job growth slowing, mortgage rates rising and unemployment climbing, only reinforced the difficulties of the national environment for Republicans.

To be sure, a wave of red cash could save Republican seats. But it’s also clear that Democrats are playing hard on their turf.

Republicans have made some significant moves on the Senate map.

The Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican Senate super PAC, pulled money from North Carolina, a sign that some top party strategists doubt that Michael Whatley can defeat former Governor Roy Cooper in the perennial battleground state. Even Trump, who tapped Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman, to run for the seat, said he was “worried about him” on Friday before leaving for his campaign swing.

The group made its first investment in Kansas, where Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican seeking a second term, appears increasingly embattled. The more than $10 million in ad reservations comes as both sides increasingly view Kansas as a late-breaking battleground. Democrats are considering spending there to support Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor and Democratic challenger.

In Texas, Republican spending smashed records as the party frantically tried to boost Ken Paxton, the scandal-tarred attorney general running for Senate. This week, Trump will host a rally in San Antonio — his second trip to Texas in two weeks, and an indication of the party’s worry about a seat it has held since 1961.

The House map keeps growing and growing for Democrats.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added eight districts to its list of seats to flip on Friday and six more on Monday, pushing the total number of competitive districts for the party to 72.

The committee expanded its electoral frontier deeper into Republican areas, adding races that included seats in rural Nevada, Virginia and Oklahoma, along with districts in Florida, Tennessee and Texas that were redrawn to favor Republicans. All 14 seats were considered safely Republican when the midterm campaign began in earnest at the start of the year.

The expansion comes a week after The Cook Political Report shifted 15 races toward Democrats, creating three new “tossup” districts in conservative swaths of North Carolina, Texas and Florida.

The campaign arm of House Democrats is planning to spend $13 million in the coming week in 35 House districts, according to an ad-buy plan shared with The New York Times.

Sources: Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (districts); Cook Political Report (race ratings)

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

The spending includes some new districts, most notably Pennsylvania’s First Congressional District, a seat held by Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, one of the only Republicans seeking re-election in a seat that President Trump lost in 2024. The other new districts are California’s 48th, Michigan’s Fourth and Seventh, and New York’s 19th.

Of the races the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is spending in, most are on offense. The party is spending on 21 seats currently held by Republicans and 14 held by Democrats.

The average 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage, the most popular home loan in the United States, rose to 7.28 percent, according to the mortgage financing giant Freddie Mac. That’s the highest since November 2023.

Strategists on both sides of the aisle were buzzing after a report on Thursday that Paxton told a group of conservative donors and lobbyists that Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas had hurt him politically.

“Do you feel like he’s a little bit of a drag?” Paxton is heard being asked in an audio recording obtained by The New York Times.

Paxton responded: “So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.”

What captivated Republicans about the report was simple: Paxton, a longtime Trump loyalist, said aloud what they were all whispering but didn’t dare say for fear of provoking the president.

Paxton just had the misfortune of being caught on tape.

84 percent.

That’s the percentage of independent voters who disapprove of Trump’s handling of gas prices, according to the NYT/Siena poll released on Saturday — a figure that has alarmed Republicans.

Hispanic voters along the border are voicing frustration with the president’s approach to immigration and the economy, raising questions about whether Republicans could lose districts in South Texas that the party redrew to tilt in their favor.

Ariel Salinas, the owner of a construction company in McAllen, Texas, blamed the president’s immigration crackdown for his inability to reliably find laborers for his work crews.

“Years ago, you put a fence up because people were stealing stuff. Now you put the fence up because ICE is stealing the workers. There was even a fence shortage in the summer. It caught all of us off guard,” he said.

“It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president. At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans. That’s what I’m going to keep on doing.” — Vice President JD Vance

“In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure. So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes. I’m going to keep focusing on the midterms and helping us win on Election Day in the next 30 days.” — Senator Ted Cruz

Vance and Cruz, two potential presidential candidates, engaged in a bit of early 2028 sniping last week, trading barbs about their midterm campaign schedules. Vance suggested that Cruz was more focused on laying the groundwork for a 2028 primary bid than helping Republicans win the coming midterm elections. Two days later, Cruz shot back, brushing off Vance’s jab.

item.title: Family of Epstein Victim Appears in Ad Targeting Republican
item.description:
A Democrat running for Congress in a competitive Colorado district released an ad on Monday that features the family of Virginia Giuffre, one of the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein’s most prominent victims.

The ad is squarely pointed at Representative Jeff Crank, criticizing him for blocking the release of federal files related to Mr. Epstein and accusing him of refusing to meet with Ms. Giuffre’s relatives.

“Jeff Crank covered up Epstein’s crimes to protect Donald Trump,” says Sky Roberts, the brother of Ms. Giuffre, who died by suicide last year. “He has no business being in Congress.”

Mr. Roberts and his wife, Amanda, who is also featured in the spot, are constituents of Mr. Crank, a Republican who is facing a tough re-election race against Jessica Killin, an Army veteran and former congressional aide to Democratic lawmakers.

Mr. Epstein and his crimes have emerged as a major issue in this year’s midterm races, as candidates across the country hammer their opponents over their positions on releasing the files and their ties to donors and supporters associated with him.

A New York Times analysis identified at least 35 congressional races with TV or digital ads that mentioned “Epstein” since January 2026. Many featured candidates running against what they called the “Epstein class.”

But the ad in Colorado’s Fifth Congressional District is unique because it features testimony from family members of one of Mr. Epstein’s most well-known victims.

Speaking directly to the camera, the couple say they have repeatedly asked to see Mr. Crank but were refused. The spot concludes with an image of their meeting with Ms. Killin.

“When he had the chance to expose the truth and release the Epstein files, he repeatedly voted to cover them up,” Ms. Roberts says in the ad.

Mr. Crank did not sign onto the bipartisan discharge petition that helped forced a vote on the release of the files, and he voted to block consideration of the Epstein Files Transparency Act on the House floor. In the final vote, however, Mr. Crank joined nearly every member of the House to approve the legislation.

A spokesman for Mr. Crank’s campaign could not immediately be reached for comment.

In an interview, the couple said they eventually met with Mr. Crank’s district director. They also joined protests against Mr. Crank and participated in news conferences outside his Colorado Springs office urging him to advocate for more transparency around the files.

They were driven by Ms. Giuffre’s death and a desire to continue her fight to expose Mr. Epstein, they say in the ad. They were pushing Mr. Crank to sign the bipartisan discharge petition that would clear the path for the legislation to come to the floor for a vote.

Mr. Roberts, who said he identifies as an independent, said they spoke with about 20 lawmakers from both parties. But not Mr. Crank.

“At the end of the day, the bare minimum of this job in this role is to hear your constituents,” said Ms. Roberts. “How can you stay with your constituents and vote according to their needs if you have no idea what their needs are?”

Ms. Giuffre was the first of Mr. Epstein’s victims to go public, which she did years after anonymously suing him and Ghislaine Maxwell, his co-conspirator, for recruiting her to join his sex-trafficking ring when she was a minor.

She accused Mr. Epstein and Ms. Maxwell of forcing her to have sex with Prince Andrew, now known as Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, and later accused him of battery and sexual assault. He flatly denied the accusations, but he relinquished his royal duties in 2019 amid the public firestorm. Earlier this year, he was arrested in connection with an investigation into accusations of misconduct in public office related to his links to Mr. Epstein.

With the ad, Democrats are seeking an edge in a race that has grown increasingly competitive, as the national environment has turned against Republican incumbents.

Republicans have held the fast-growing, Colorado Springs-area district since its creation in 1973. But, this year, Democrats have included the race on their list of targets, a sign that the party believes Ms. Killin can flip the seat.

item.title: California Prepares to Ban Quartz Countertop Production
item.description:
California is set to become the first state to ban the production or installation of man-made quartz, amid mounting cases of a lethal lung disease among workers who carve the material for kitchen countertops.

The emergency regulation, which California’s Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board is expected to pass in October, signals growing alarm over the ill effects of a popular alternative to granite and marble.

The board, made up of health, labor and corporate leaders, unanimously agreed in May to take up the proposed ban, which would target manufactured stone that contains more than 1 percent of crystalline silica. The rule would be subject to brief state review before taking effect.

Man-made quartz is packed with crystalline silica, which is released as dust into the air when a slab is cut. The particles lodge in the lungs, prompting an aggressive immune response; scar tissue forms, slowly killing the lung. By the time silicosis is diagnosed, patients often need a single or double lung transplant.

Representatives for manufacturers and distributors in the $30 billion engineered-stone industry say quartz is safe. They blame fabrication workshops further down the chain of production, where engineered stone slabs are cut to spec, for the surge in silicosis cases.

There are many such fabrication workshops in California. Many of the workers have tenuous immigration status. Since 2019, California has confirmed 657 silicosis cases and 35 silicosis-related deaths among countertop workers, according to the state’s Department of Public Health. The state has also recorded a rising tide of lawsuits for injuries related to stone cutting, with multimillion-dollar verdicts. The workers, along with their lawyers, doctors and occupational health experts, have said there is no safe way to cut quartz.

California’s ban would be an acknowledgment that the state’s laws requiring safer processing techniques for quartz are not enough to protect workers: Compliance is too low and the industry too fragmented, with many small shops that escape inspection, according to the California Department of Industrial Relations, which has pushed for the ban.

“The standards board’s decision reflects the urgent need to protect workers from a product that has proven uniquely hazardous,” said Denisse Gómez, a spokeswoman for the department.

“Cal-OSHA issuing this rule sends a message to other OSHA programs,” said Dr. David Michaels, an epidemiologist at George Washington University’s school of public health who ran the federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration from 2009 to 2017. “But it also sends a strong signal to the countertop markets. It tells consumers and countertop manufacturers and big-box stores that they all must shift to a safer alternative.”

Engineered stone can also be produced with recycled glass and other materials that are considered safer. Australia banned quartz countertops in 2024, with a total import ban starting in 2025.

Most quartz slabs sold in the United States come from overseas manufacturers and reach American homes through a network of home improvement stores and smaller distributors, passing through fabrication shops where they are cut for kitchens and bathrooms.

The largest U.S. manufacturer of engineered stone is Cambria, a family-owned company in Minnesota. The company has fought against the lawsuits filed by workers with silicosis, and has lobbied members of Congress for support. A quartz ban in California could hurt Cambria because of the state’s large market and because Cal-OSHA often sets the pace for other states.

In January, Cambria’s chief legal officer testified at a House subcommittee in support of a bill that would shield engineered stone from liability in lawsuits involving injuries, putting it in the same protected category as vaccines and firearms.

“The problem is the process, not the product,” Rebecca Shult, the company’s lawyer, told lawmakers.

Other states have also raised the alarm about silicosis in people working with engineered stone. Last month, New York City’s health department issued an advisory to health care workers, alerting them to recent cases in the state. In December, Massachusetts issued a public health advisory on silica dust, calling it “a respiratory hazard for stone manufacturers.”

item.title: Kash Patel Is Engaged to Country Singer Alexis Wilkins
item.description:
The director of the F.B.I. is getting hitched.

Kash Patel, 46, and his girlfriend, Alexis Wilkins, 27, announced their engagement on their social media accounts on Sunday with heart and ring emojis.

“Went and got the law involved,” Ms. Wilkins posted on X, along with a black and white picture of the couple in which she shows her ring.

Mr. Patel, who became F.B.I. director in February 2025, and Ms. Wilkins met in the fall of 2022 at a party at the Nashville home of the country music artist John Rich. The event was a celebration of the release of Mr. Rich’s song “Progress” on President Trump’s Truth Social platform.

At that time, Mr. Patel, who had been an aide in the president’s first term, was a Truth Social consultant opining on conservative podcasts and selling merchandise branded “K$H”-and children’s books praising “King Donald.”

A publicist had brought Ms. Wilkins, who was living in Nashville, to the party. Mr. Patel complimented Ms. Wilkins on the jacket she was wearing that night. By early 2023, the couple were dating.

Their relationship became better known in Washington in early 2025, when Ms. Wilkins sat in the gallery during Mr. Patel’s Senate confirmation hearing.

“I just liked that he was so honest,” Ms. Wilkins said on “The Megan Kelly Show” last year. “His character is incredible, his values are incredible.”

Their relationship has also drawn scrutiny — including from inside the Trump administration — over Mr. Patel’s use of government jets and F.B.I. agents for himself and Ms. Wilkins.

F.B.I. tactical agents ferried Ms. Wilkins to a resort in Britain before a dinner at Windsor Castle last year, and at another time to an appointment at a hair salon in Nashville. In another instance, agents in two S.U.V.s stood guard outside a senior center in Ronald Reagan’s boyhood hometown of Dixon, Ill., as Ms. Wilkins performed for a group of young conservatives.

item.title: This High-Profile Campaign May Be the Ugliest in the Country
item.description:
Of all the mudslinging and smear campaigning across the country in this fraught election year, few races are as nasty as the one for governor of Ohio.

Dr. Amy Acton, a Democrat who was once the state’s chief public health officer, holds a narrow lead against Vivek Ramaswamy, a Republican who made a mint in pharmaceutical start-ups, according to a New York Times and Siena University poll released on Sunday.

The two candidates differ significantly on policy matters, but their campaign advertisements, mailers and social media have not all been about substance.

Instead, voters might think one candidate is a con artist; the other is a drunk.

“It’s definitely ugly,” said Christopher Gagin, the former chairman of the Belmont County Republican Party. In past races, he and others said, even hard-hitting attack ads were mostly based on issues or a candidate’s past performance in office. “This,” Mr. Gagin said, “is all very, very personal.”

As is often the case, the campaign attacks in Ohio might be based on actual events, but the sound bites are hardly the full stories. Voters might actually be tuning out all the toxicity.

Dr. Acton, who has faced an onslaught of attacks maligning her as a violent pill popper, is viewed more favorably than unfavorably by voters, according to the Times/Siena poll. Mr. Ramaswamy, who has been accused of making millions by swindling everyday Ohioans, is viewed more unfavorably than favorably, but by a narrow margin not much different from surveys taken months ago.

And there are few signs that the specific nature of the attacks is undermining traditional partisan loyalties.

Despite being painted as an out-of-touch billionaire, Mr. Ramaswamy has a healthy lead among Ohioans without college degrees, as would be expected for any Republican these days. Dr. Acton, painted as scandalously underqualified, has an even larger lead among Ohioans with college degrees, a reliable Democratic constituency.

Still, even if the voters are ignoring them, the ads are unquestionably nasty, especially the ones launched by groups backing Mr. Ramaswamy that aim at Dr. Acton.

“Ohio is not new to negative advertising, but typically that revolves around issues or maybe tying candidates to unpopular national figures,” said Robert Alexander, a professor at Bowling Green State University in northwest Ohio who directs a statewide poll. “But the personal nature, particularly of those anti-Acton ads, have been somewhat alarming.”

Ramaswamy backers are outspending the Acton camp on advertising by a more than three-to-one margin, and many of their ads have inflated the events of a single night in the Columbus suburbs in late August 2019.

A daughter of Dr. Acton’s called 911 to say that her stepfather and her mother were fighting and that her mother had been “drinking and throwing things.” In an incident report, a police officer who came to the house wrote that Dr. Acton and her husband had been arguing about her long work hours and that in the course of the argument she “grabbed hold of a mirror on the wall and pulled it down,” breaking the glass. The officer wrote that the two had been drinking and that she had taken medication.

The police left and nothing came of it — until it was reported by NBC News this past April. Dr. Acton’s husband, Eric Acton, said in a statement that his wife had a single drink that night and that the argument, which he said he had started, was over before the police showed up. The Acton campaign said the prescription medications were for migraines and high blood pressure. As for the mirror, she bumped into it, knocking it off the wall, the campaign said.

But the incident has become something of a foundational text for a vicious oeuvre of attacks. The state Republican Party has described Dr. Acton as “violent,” and “unstable,” posting computer-generated images of her jeep with a license plate that reads “Drunk Mom” or staring into a broken mirror on which is written, in blood-red lettering, “Mom has been drinking.”

“Amy Acton: Drinking. Drugs. Disaster. Disqualified,” said one ad among many, showing a spilled wine glass, an empty pill bottle and a woman passed out on a couch.

Candidates typically turn negative when they are down in the polls, and the Times/Siena poll has been among several recent surveys showing Mr. Ramaswamy narrowly behind. But, Professor Alexander said, the main problem facing Republicans this year is a discouraged electorate, and it’s unclear that this strategy would fix that.

“Are you really inspiring people with those kinds of attacks?” he asked.

Jai Chabria, chief strategist for the Ramaswamy campaign, pointed out that these ads were from outside spending groups, not the campaign itself, but he defended their content.

“The instances that are described in those ads are factual, and they point to a person who doesn’t have the capability to take on a chief executive role,” he said. “I think it’s completely fair.”

The Acton campaign cited the “baseless lies about her and her family” as the reason Dr. Acton was not going to debate Mr. Ramaswamy.

The Democrats’ counteroffensive has not been as intensely personal, directing its fire instead at Mr. Ramaswamy’s business history and ample wealth. But the hits have been nasty all the same.

Ads have called Mr. Ramaswamy a “con man” and a “swindler,” emphasizing the millions he made pitching his pharmaceutical start-ups and suggesting criminality that authorities have not alleged. One prominent ad features a widower whose wife had suffered from Alzheimer’s disease, accusing Mr. Ramaswamy of making “hundreds of millions of dollars scamming people like me.”

(The ad is not dissimilar to an ad from the Ramaswamy campaign, in which a woman says she would never forgive Dr. Acton for the fact that her mother died alone during Covid lockdowns. But an obituary surfaced by a progressive Ohio outlet showed that the woman’s mother died in Kentucky, six weeks after Dr. Acton had left state government in Ohio.)

While the anti-Ramaswamy ad does not make clear precisely how the man believes he was scammed, it is referring to Axovant, one of Mr. Ramaswamy’s pharmaceutical companies.

Axovant, which employed eight people, including Mr. Ramaswamy’s mother and brother, both physicians, was founded to bring to market an Alzheimer’s drug that the pharmaceutical giant GlaxoSmithKline had given up on after four failed clinical trials.

Mr. Ramaswamy talked up the drug, intepirdine, wherever he could, portraying it as a potential breakthrough that “could help millions” of people. Then, six months after buying the drug, he took Axovant public in a debut that sent the company’s market value soaring to nearly $3 billion.

In late 2015, Mr. Ramaswamy sold off a portion of Axovant’s parent company, Roivant, claiming more than $37 million in capital gains on his tax return that year. In August 2017, he secured another big payday for Roivant when the Japanese conglomerate SoftBank led an investment of $1.1 billion in Roivant, which had a broad portfolio of pharmaceuticals. A few weeks later, intepirdine failed in a clinical trial and Axovant stock plunged.

The Acton camp has framed these events as a classic “pump and dump” that made Mr. Ramaswamy hugely rich while fleecing regular folks in the form of pension funds and retirement investments.

Mr. Ramaswamy has strongly denied such claims, saying if he had held onto the Roivant shares he sold, he would have made money. In an interview with The Times during his failed presidential campaign in 2023, he said criticism of his actions “grates on me a little bit.”

But in the ugly Ohio race, that criticism has taken center stage.

“Vivek Ramaswamy is a billionaire scam artist who pumped up an Alzheimer's drug that he knew didn’t work, gave false hope to millions of impacted families, and cashed out days before the drug failed,” Addie Bullock, a spokeswoman for the Acton campaign, wrote in an email. “Now, he’s running a disgusting smear campaign riddled with ads that have been condemned as ‘defamatory’ and ‘vile’.”
